unmatched_peer.body: `markcoroutinefunction(self)` marks the *instance* as a coroutine function, but Django's signal dispatch checks `iscoroutinefunction` on the callable itself. Because `AsyncHandler` has a coroutine `__call__`, `iscoroutinefunction` already returns `True` for instances without any extra marking. More importantly, each test creates a new `AsyncHandler()` instance, and `markcoroutinefunction` sets a `_is_coroutine` attribute on that specific instance — but the function being dispatched is `__call__`, not the instance. This may or may not match the original intent of the removed `_is_coroutine = asyncio.coroutines._is_coroutine` class-level attribute. The correct usage of `markcoroutinefunction` is to call it on the callable that needs marking: `markcoroutinefunction(AsyncHandler)` (on the class) or `markcoroutinefunction(AsyncHandler.__call__)`. Marking the instance (`self`) instead of the class or its `__call__` method is unlikely to have the intended effect.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The original code set `_is_coroutine = asyncio.coroutines._is_coroutine` as a class attribute, which made `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction()` return `True` for any instance. `markcoroutinefunction(self)` sets that attribute on the instance, but `asgiref.sync.iscoroutinefunction` (used by Django's dispatcher) checks `_is_coroutine` on the object passed — for a callable instance that is the instance itself, so it may work, but it differs from `markcoroutinefunction(AsyncHandler)` (class-level). Marking the class is the idiomatic replacement for the old class-attribute pattern.
